unit.title: Undertake fabrication, forming, bending and shaping – (basic)

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A sheet metal box has four bends. Why is the bending order planned before the first bend is made?
options: So the press brake does not need a back gauge
So that every bend can use the same bend angle
So the sheet can be cut to size after bending
So earlier flanges do not foul the tools on later bends

questions.stem: Why is a 'first-off' part made and checked before a batch of 50 brackets is bent?
options: To use up the offcuts before the job begins
To prove the set-up is right before the rest are made
So the operator can practise on the customer's part
To warm up the press brake before the real job

questions.stem: A drawing shows the outside sizes of a bent bracket. What must you work out before cutting the blank?
options: The flat length, allowing for the bends
Nothing; the blank is the sum of the outside sizes
Only the weight of the finished part
The welding current for the bracket

questions.stem: Which document tells the operator the material, thickness, bend angles and order of bends for a part?
options: The delivery note from the steel supplier
The machine's electrical wiring diagram
The drawing and the job or process sheet
The workshop's cleaning schedule

questions.stem: A job needs 40 identical brackets bent at 90°. What helps make every bend in the same place?
options: Set the back gauge and check it on the first part
Mark every blank by eye with a rough soapstone line
Ask a different trainee to bend each bracket
Bend each part by hand over the bench edge

questions.stem: A press brake has a light curtain. A trainee wants to switch it off because it 'keeps stopping the machine'. What should you do?
options: Allow it, if he promises to keep his hands clear
Switch it off for small parts only
Refuse, and find out why it keeps tripping
Tape over one sensor so it trips less often

questions.stem: Before the top tool of a press brake is changed, what must be done?
options: Lower the ram slowly to check the gap by hand
Leave it running at slow speed so it can be moved
Switch off at the pedal and leave the power on
Isolate and lock off, and support the tool

questions.stem: Why should the operator stand clear of a large sheet, and support it, as a bend is made on a press brake?
options: The sheet gets hot and can burn the hands
The sheet whips up fast and can hit you
The sheet may stick to the top tool after bending
The sheet makes a loud noise as it bends

questions.stem: On bending rolls, why is a long plate fed with the help of a crane or a second person at the far end?
options: To carry its weight as it curves up and over
To stop the rolls turning the wrong way
So no pre-bend is needed on the plate
To hold the plate flat so it does not curve

questions.stem: Which is the best way to stop fingers being trapped when small parts are fed into a press brake?
options: Wear thick gloves so the tool cannot hurt you
Work faster so your hands are in the tools less
Hold the part at its very edge, close to the tool
Use a holding tool, with hands outside the guard

questions.stem: A trainee reaches under the guard of a guillotine to straighten a sheet. What should you do as the supervisor?
options: Nothing, as long as his foot is off the pedal
Tell him to do it faster next time
Stop him and show him the safe way
Raise the guard higher so he can reach more easily

questions.stem: Why does stainless steel usually need more force and more overbend than mild steel of the same thickness?
options: It is softer, so it bends further than you want
It is stronger and work-hardens as it bends
It conducts heat away from the bend line
It has no grain, so it cannot be bent cold

questions.stem: Some aluminium sheet cracks when it is bent tightly. What is usually done?
options: Use a larger inside radius, or a softer temper
Bend it faster so it has no time to crack
Use a smaller inside radius to pinch the crack
Cool it in water before bending

questions.stem: Why should steel not be bent while it is at a 'blue heat' (a few hundred degrees Celsius)?
options: It is too soft and will tear apart
It will turn bright and lose its scale
It will harden and become a spring
It is more brittle then and may crack

questions.stem: Why might a part be stress relieved (heated and cooled slowly) after heavy cold forming?
options: To make it much harder and more wear-resistant
To change the colour so it can be painted
To reduce stresses locked in by the forming
To make it springier, like a spring

questions.stem: What happens to the thickness of the metal on the outside of a tight bend?
options: It gets thicker, as the metal is squeezed
It gets thinner, as the metal is stretched
It stays exactly the same all the way round
It doubles, because the sheet folds over

questions.stem: A 90° bend in 2 mm sheet has an inside radius of 4 mm. Taking the neutral axis at mid-thickness, what is the bend allowance? (Bend allowance = 1.571 × neutral radius)
options: 6.3 mm
9.4 mm
7.9 mm
3.1 mm

questions.stem: An L-bracket has flat legs of 50 mm and 30 mm, measured to where the bend starts, and a bend allowance of 7.9 mm. What blank length is needed?
Because of springback, a bend comes out at 92° when 90° is needed. What is the usual fix?
options: Set the bend to 92° next time
Heat the bend and hammer it
Use a thinner sheet for the job
Overbend about 2°, to about 88°

questions.stem: A common guide for air bending mild steel uses a V-die opening of about 8 times the sheet thickness. Which opening suits 3 mm sheet?
options: 12 mm
24 mm
8 mm
48 mm

questions.stem: A pipe is bent to 90° on a centre-line radius of 150 mm. About how long is the pipe along the curved part? (Arc length = 1.571 × radius)
options: About 236 mm
About 150 mm
About 471 mm
About 300 mm

questions.stem: A rolled cylinder should be 500 mm in diameter. It measures 506 mm one way and 494 mm the other. What is the out-of-roundness as a percentage of 500 mm?
With the same die, the force needed to bend sheet rises with the square of its thickness. If the thickness is doubled, about how much more force is needed?
options: The same force
Twice the force
Three times the force
Four times the force

questions.stem: Why does a very short flange, close to the bend line, often fail to bend properly on a press brake?
options: The flange is too stiff to bend at all
It does not reach across the V-die opening
The top tool is always much too narrow for it
Short flanges spring back to flat

questions.stem: What is the main difference between air bending and bottoming on a press brake?
options: Air bending needs no die; bottoming needs no punch
Air bending uses compressed air to push the sheet down
In air bending, the sheet never touches the die floor
Bottoming is only used for aluminium sheet

questions.stem: In air bending on a press brake, how is the bend angle mostly controlled?
options: By how deep the punch goes into the die
By the shape of the die alone, every time
By the position of the back gauge
By the speed at which the punch comes down

questions.stem: Which machine is the best choice for bending a 10 mm thick steel plate bracket to 90° cold?
options: A hand box and pan folder
A set of bending rolls
A hand seamer
A press brake

questions.stem: Why is a small relief cut made at the end of a bend line where a flange meets an edge that is not bent?
options: To make the finished part lighter in weight
To stop the metal tearing at the corner
To mark where the back gauge goes
To let the paint run into the corner

questions.stem: A cylinder rolled on a three-roll machine has come out cone-shaped (wider at one end). What is the likely cause?
options: The rolls were not set parallel to each other
The plate was cut much too long for the cylinder
The ends were pre-bent before rolling
The plate was rolled too slowly

questions.stem: After a rolled cylinder is welded, the seam has a point (peaking) instead of a smooth curve. What is the usual cause?
options: The weld was made with too low a current
The cylinder was rolled too round
The plate ends were not pre-bent enough
The seam was ground flush after welding

questions.stem: Why is a template held against a cylinder after each pass while it is being rolled?
options: To measure how thick the plate is
To check that the plate has no rust or scale
To find the weight of the cylinder
To stop it before it rolls too tight

questions.stem: When a pipe is cold bent to too tight a radius, what usually happens?
options: The outside wall becomes thicker
The inside wrinkles and the pipe goes oval
The pipe gets longer by the bend allowance
Nothing, as pipe can bend to any radius

questions.stem: Why is a mandrel (an inside support) used when bending thin-walled tube to a tight radius?
options: To heat the tube from the inside as it bends
To measure the angle of the bend from inside
To stop the tube flattening and wrinkling
To make the tube thicker on the outside

questions.stem: Angle iron is to be bent to a square corner for a frame. What is usually done first?
options: Cut a 90° V-notch out of one leg at the bend line
Heat the whole length of the bar to a bright red heat
Roll the bar into a ring, then cut it
Drill a row of holes along both legs

questions.stem: When angle iron is rolled into a ring, what can happen to the leg on the inside of the curve?
options: It is stretched and gets thinner
It is squeezed and may buckle or wave
It turns hard and snaps at once
It stays the same as the outer leg

questions.stem: A 25 mm round steel bar is to be hot bent. How hot should it be?
options: Black heat, just warm to the touch
White hot, with sparks coming off
Dull blue, a few hundred degrees
An even bright red over the bend

questions.stem: Steel is heated until it gives off bright sparks and its surface bubbles. What has happened?
options: It is burnt and must be scrapped
It is at just the right heat for bending
It is now harder and stronger
The scale has protected it

questions.stem: Why is a long hot-formed part left to cool slowly in still air, and not thrown into water?
options: Water makes the scale too hard to remove
Air cooling makes the part grow longer
Fast, uneven cooling can distort and crack it
Water would turn the steel to stainless

questions.stem: Which tool is best for checking the inside radius of a bend against the drawing?
options: A steel rule
A radius gauge
A feeler gauge
A spirit level

questions.stem: A drawing gives a bend angle of 90° ± 1°. Which measured angle is outside the tolerance?
A long bend made on a press brake is 90° at the ends but 92° in the middle. What is the likely cause?
options: The ram and bed deflect (bow) under load
The sheet was too short for the machine
The back gauge was set at the wrong distance
The middle of the sheet was colder than the ends

questions.stem: A batch of formed parts is found to be 3 mm short on one flange. Before changing anything, what should you check first?
options: The colour of the paint on the parts
The weight of each part in the batch
The blank sizes and the back gauge setting
Which trainee made them, so they can be blamed

questions.stem: A trainee you supervise is about to roll a cylinder without pre-bending the ends. What is the best action?
options: Let him go on and learn from his mistake
Stop him, explain why, and show the pre-bend
Pre-bend them yourself later, without saying a word
Tell him to grind the flats off afterwards

questions.stem: Which details should be written on the job card when a batch of formed parts is finished?
options: Only the time the job finished
The weather on the day and each lunch break taken
The machine's purchase price and supplier
Quantity, checks made, results and any rejects

questions.stem: A customer asks for a change to a bend angle after the job has started. What should you do?
options: Get the change in writing and update the drawing
Change it on the parts not yet bent, and say nothing
Refuse, because a job can never be changed once started
Change it on the machine and keep the old drawing

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name for slightly bowing a press brake's bed or tools so that a long bend has the same angle all along it?
What is the factor called that gives where the neutral axis lies in the thickness of a bend, often between about 0.33 and 0.5?
What is the name of the hard, flaky oxide layer that forms on steel when it is heated for hot forming?
What heat treatment, heating steel above its critical temperature and cooling it in still air, refines the grain after hot forming?
A channel has outside sizes of 25 mm, 50 mm and 25 mm. The bend deduction is 4 mm for each of its two bends. What blank length is needed, in mm?
What tool measures the angle between two faces, using an adjustable blade and a scale in degrees?
What safety control on a press brake needs both of the operator's hands on buttons before the ram will move?
What is the name for switching off a machine's power, locking the switch and fixing a tag before work is done on it?
What is the name for the gap between the top and bottom blades of a guillotine, which is set to suit the sheet thickness?
Which steel section has a cross-section shaped like a capital I or H?
Each bracket takes 3 minutes on the press brake. In a 7.5-hour day, 30 minutes are lost to setting up. How many brackets can be bent in the day?
Steel sheet weighs about 7.85 kg per square metre for each 1 mm of thickness. What does 1 square metre of 3 mm steel sheet weigh, in kg?
What is the name for hammering or pressing hot steel into shape, as a blacksmith does?
Which word describes a metal that can be bent or stretched a long way without cracking?
What is the name of the clamps on a guillotine that come down to hold the sheet still just before the blade cuts?

essays.stem: You must make 25 identical steel channel brackets on a press brake. Explain how you would plan the job: the blank size, the tooling, the bending order, the first-off check and the records.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the drawing for the material, the thickness, the sizes, the bend angles, the inside radius and the tolerances, and check that the material is in stock. I work out the blank length from the bend allowance, or from the bend deduction chart for our tools, and make a cutting list for 25 blanks plus one or two spares for setting up. I choose the punch and V-die to suit the thickness and the radius, check the machine's force chart, and plan the bending order so that the first flange does not hit the tools on the second bend. I set the back gauge and bend one first-off part. I check it fully against the drawing: the angles with a protractor, the flange lengths, the radius and the squareness. If it is right, it is signed off and kept as the sample; if not, I adjust and make another. During the run, parts are checked at set intervals, such as every fifth part. I record the blank size, tooling, settings, first-off result, checks and any rejects on the job card so the job can be repeated.
markingPoints: Reads the drawing for material, thickness, sizes, angles, radius and tolerances
Works out the blank length (bend allowance or deduction) and a cutting list with spares
Chooses tooling, checks the force chart, and plans the bending order
Bends and fully checks a first-off part, and signs it off as the sample
Checks during the run and records settings, results and rejects

essays.stem: Explain how a fabricator works out the blank length for a part with a bend. Use a worked example: a 90° bend in 4 mm sheet with an inside radius of 6 mm, and straight legs of 40 mm and 60 mm measured to where the bend starts. Take the neutral axis at mid-thickness.
essays.modelAnswer: When metal is bent, the outside stretches and the inside is squeezed. In between is the neutral axis, which stays the same length, so the blank length is worked out along it. For a fairly large radius it is taken at about the middle of the thickness. The length of metal in the bend, the bend allowance, is the length of the neutral axis arc. For a 90° bend this is a quarter of a circle: 2 × π × r ÷ 4, or about 1.571 × r, where r is the neutral radius. In the example, the neutral radius is 6 + (4 ÷ 2) = 8 mm. The bend allowance is 1.571 × 8 = 12.6 mm (12.57 mm). The straight legs are 40 mm and 60 mm, so the blank length is 40 + 60 + 12.6 = 112.6 mm. In practice I check the result with a test bend, because on tight bends the neutral axis moves towards the inside, and I use the shop's bend chart where there is one.
markingPoints: Explains the neutral axis: it does not stretch, so the blank is measured along it
Bend allowance is the neutral-axis arc: about 1.571 × neutral radius for 90°
Neutral radius 6 + 2 = 8 mm
Bend allowance about 12.6 mm; blank 40 + 60 + 12.6 = 112.6 mm
Checks with a test bend or the shop's bend chart

essays.stem: As the person in charge of a press brake, explain how you would make sure it is used safely by a team of trainees, including the guards, the set-up, tool changes and supervision.
essays.modelAnswer: Before anyone uses the press brake I make sure they have been trained and know the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules. At the start of each session I check the guards and safety devices: the light curtain or other guard works and stops the ram, the two-hand control or guarded foot pedal works, and the emergency stops work. Nobody may bypass or switch off a guard. For tool changes, the machine is isolated and locked off, and the tools are supported and lifted with help or a lifting aid, because they are heavy. I check that the punch and die suit the thickness and that the force needed is within the rating of the machine and the tools. Only one person works the controls and decides when to bend. Helpers holding a large sheet keep their hands clear and stand where the sheet cannot whip up into them. Small parts are held with holding tools. I watch the team, stop any unsafe act at once, and record faults and near misses.
markingPoints: Only trained people use it, following the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Guards, two-hand control or pedal guard and emergency stops checked each session; never bypassed
Tool changes with the machine isolated and locked off, tools supported and lifted safely
Tooling and force within the machine's and tools' ratings
One operator, hands clear, sheet whip allowed for, unsafe acts stopped and faults recorded

essays.stem: Explain how the choice of material (mild steel, stainless steel or aluminium) affects how a part is bent, and what you would change for each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Mild steel is the easiest to bend. It needs a moderate force, can usually be bent to an inside radius about equal to its thickness, and springs back only a little, so a small overbend is enough. Stainless steel is stronger and work-hardens as it bends, so it needs more force (check the machine's rating), more overbend for its greater springback, and often a larger radius. Its surface must be kept free of scratches and steel particles, so clean tools, protective film and tools kept for stainless are used, or it may show rust spots later. Aluminium is soft, but some grades and tempers crack if they are bent tightly, so the inside radius must be larger, as the maker's chart gives, and the grain direction matters even more. It scratches and marks easily, so the tools are kept clean and smooth. For all three, I check the material certificate or grade, bend across the grain where possible, and make a test bend before the batch.
markingPoints: Mild steel: moderate force, small radius, little springback
Stainless: more force, more springback, work-hardens, kept free of steel contamination
Aluminium: larger radius, grade and temper matter, can crack, scratches easily
Checks the grade and bends across the grain
Makes a test bend before the batch

essays.stem: A rolled and welded cylinder is out of round and has a peaked seam. Explain the likely causes, how you would measure the faults, and how you would prevent them on the next cylinder.
essays.modelAnswer: To measure out-of-roundness, I measure the diameter in at least four directions at each end and in the middle, and compare the largest and the smallest with the tolerance. Likely causes are uneven rolling, rolling past the right curve, or flat ends left by poor pre-bending. To check for peaking, I hold a template across the seam; a point shows as a gap at the middle of the template. Peaking usually comes from ends that were not pre-bent enough, so they stayed flat, and from weld shrinkage pulling the seam in. A cone shape or a twist comes from rolls that are not parallel or a plate fed in at an angle. For the next cylinder I would check that the blank is square and the right length (mean diameter × π), pre-bend both ends fully, feed the plate square, set the rolls parallel, roll in small steps, and check with the template after each pass. I would tack the seam at even spacing with the edges held level, weld in a balanced way, check the shape again after welding, and record the measurements.
markingPoints: Measures the diameter in several directions at several positions and compares with the tolerance
Uses a template across the seam to find peaking
Causes: poor pre-bending, uneven or over-rolling, weld shrinkage, rolls not parallel
Prevention: square blank of the right length, full pre-bend, small steps, template checks, balanced tacking and welding
Records the measurements

essays.stem: Explain how flat bar or angle iron is formed into a ring or into a square frame corner, the problems that can occur (such as twist, buckling and the wrong size), and how you would prevent them.
essays.modelAnswer: To make a ring from flat bar, I work out the length along the neutral axis (the mean diameter × π), or use the shop chart for angle, and add an allowance to trim. The ring is rolled on section rolls or bent around a former in small steps, checking with a template. Angle rolled 'leg in' has the outstanding leg squeezed, so it may buckle or wave; rolled 'leg out', that leg is stretched, so it may thin or crack if the radius is tight. The bar can twist as it is rolled, so the guide rolls are set to hold it upright. To make a square corner in angle iron, I cut a 90° V-notch out of the leg that lies across the bend, bend the other leg sharply at the notch, and weld the closed notch. Problems are the wrong size, twist, buckling and cracked corners. I prevent them with a correct length calculation, small rolling steps, guide rolls set correctly, a template, and a check for twist with the part clamped on a flat table.
markingPoints: Works out the length (mean diameter or chart) with a trim allowance
Rolls or bends in small steps with template checks; guide rolls against twist
Explains leg-in buckling and leg-out stretching
Square corner: 90° V-notch in one leg, bend, weld the notch
Names problems and how each is prevented, including a twist check on a flat table

essays.stem: Explain how you would hot form a 25 mm square steel bar into a bracket with two bends, including the heating, temperature control, tools, safety and care of the finished part.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the drawing, mark the bend positions on the bar with a centre punch (soapstone burns off), and make a template or setting jig. I set up a forming area clear of anything that can burn, with a heavy vice or bending fork, a hammer, tongs and a fire extinguisher, and check the gas set. I wear tinted goggles, heat-resistant gloves, flame-resistant clothing and boots. I heat the first bend area with a heating nozzle, evenly all round the bar and over the length of the bend, to an even bright red. I do not overheat it until it sparks, as that burns the steel, and I stop bending if it cools to a blue heat, as it may crack; I reheat instead. I bend steadily with the bar held firmly and check against the template. Then I make the second bend the same way, checking that it is in the same plane as the first. I let the part cool slowly in still air, mark it as hot, clean off the scale and check it against the drawing.
markingPoints: Marks the bends with a centre punch and makes a template or jig
Safe forming area, tools and PPE; gas set checked
Heats evenly all round and over the bend length to bright red
Avoids burning the steel and bending at a blue heat; reheats as needed
Checks against the template and plane, cools in still air, marks it hot, final check

essays.stem: Describe how you would inspect a batch of formed parts (angles, radii, flange lengths, flatness and surface), the tools you would use, and how you would record and deal with parts that do not conform.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the first part fully, then a sample from the batch at set intervals, or every part if the drawing or the customer asks. I use a protractor or angle gauge for the bend angles, radius gauges for the inside radius, a steel rule, tape or vernier caliper for the flange lengths and hole positions, a square for squareness, and a straight edge or flat table with feeler gauges for flatness and twist. I look at the outside of each bend for cracks, and at the surface for tool marks, scratches and dents, especially on stainless steel and aluminium. I compare each result with the drawing tolerance and record it on an inspection sheet with the part number, the measurements, pass or fail, the date and my name. A part that fails is given a reject tag and kept apart so that it cannot be mixed with good parts. I report it, find the cause (blank size, back gauge, tooling or material), and decide with the supervisor whether it can be reworked or must be scrapped.
markingPoints: First part checked fully, then a sample at set intervals
Right tools: protractor, radius gauge, rule or caliper, square, straight edge and feeler gauges
Checks bends for cracks and the surface for marks
Records results against the tolerance on an inspection sheet
Non-conforming parts tagged, kept apart, reported, cause found, rework or scrap decided

essays.stem: Explain how you would train and supervise a new team member to use plate bending rolls safely and correctly.
essays.modelAnswer: First I explain the hazards: the nip between the rolls can draw in hands, gloves, sleeves and rags, and plates are heavy and sharp. I show the guards, the trip bar and the emergency stops, and test them with the trainee. I explain the controls and how to set the rolls parallel and adjust them for the plate thickness. Then I demonstrate: check that the blank is square and the right length, pre-bend both ends, feed the plate in square, roll a little at a time and check with a template. I make sure loose clothing is tied back, that gloves are not worn near the nip if the Centre's rules say so, and that a second person or a crane supports long plates. Then the trainee does each step while I watch, starting on a small plate. I correct mistakes straight away, ask questions to check understanding, and only let the trainee work alone once they show they are safe and competent. I record the training and sign it off.
markingPoints: Explains the hazards: the nip, heavy and sharp plate
Shows and tests the guards, trip bar and emergency stops
Demonstrates the method: square blank, pre-bend, square feed, small steps, template
Trainee practises under close supervision, with corrections and questions
Signs off only when competent, and records the training

essays.stem: Many parts in a batch have cracked on the outside of the bend. Explain how you would investigate the cause, and what you would report and recommend.
essays.modelAnswer: First I stop the batch and quarantine all the parts, good and bad, so that no cracked part is sent out. I count and record how many are cracked and where the cracks are. I check the drawing and the work: was the inside radius smaller than the drawing or the material chart allows? Were the bends made along the grain instead of across it? Were the cut edges burred or rough at the bend, which starts cracks? I check the material certificate to see whether the right grade and temper were used, or whether a harder material was supplied. I check the tooling: a worn or very sharp punch, or a V-die that is too narrow, gives too tight a radius. I make test bends to prove the cause. My report gives the job, the number of parts affected, what I found, the cause, what was done with the parts, and my recommendations, such as a larger radius, bending across the grain, deburring the edges, or changing the tooling or the material.
markingPoints: Stops the batch and quarantines the parts; records how many and where
Checks the inside radius against what is allowed, and the grain direction
Checks the material certificate (grade and temper) and the edges and tooling
Proves the cause with test bends
Report with findings, cause, action taken and recommendations

practical1.title: Planning and forming a batch of channel brackets, with first-off and batch inspection
practical1.brief: Your group must make a batch of ten channel brackets in 2 mm mild steel to the assessor's drawing (for example 30 mm × 60 mm × 30 mm outside, 150 mm long, with bends of 90° ± 1°). If the Centre has no press brake, use the box and pan folder and the sheet thickness the assessor gives. First, as a group, work out the blank size using the bend allowance or the bend deduction for the Centre's tools (show the working), write a cutting list, choose the tools and plan the bending order. One member leads the set-up and the first-off check; another member leads the batch inspection. Cut the blanks on the guillotine and deburr them. Set the back gauge, bend one first-off bracket and check it fully against the drawing; adjust and repeat until it passes, then sign it off as the sample. Every member then bends at least two brackets while the assessor watches, and checks and records another member's parts on the inspection sheet (angles, flange sizes, length and squareness). Tag and set aside any part that fails, and write down its likely cause. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the calculation, plan, inspection sheet and photos once for the whole group.
materials: 2 mm mild steel sheet, enough for 12 blanks
Press brake with a punch and V-die to suit 2 mm sheet (or a box and pan folder)
Protractor, radius gauges, steel rule, vernier caliper and engineer's square
Calculation sheet, inspection sheet and reject tags
photos: The calculation, cutting list and bending plan
The blanks cut, deburred and counted
The machine set up, with the guards and emergency stop checked
The first-off bracket being measured with the protractor
A member bending a bracket with hands clear of the tools
The finished batch laid out, with any rejects tagged
checklist: Helped work out the blank size and can explain the bend allowance or deduction used
Checked the guards and emergency stop and set up safely before bending
Cut and deburred blanks to size within the tolerance
Bent own brackets in the planned order, with hands clear of the tools
Measured another member's parts accurately and recorded the results honestly
Found any failed part and gave a likely cause
Wore safety glasses, boots and suitable gloves for handling sheet
Left the machines isolated and the area clean
safety: Never bypass or switch off a guard or light curtain; test the emergency stop before use
Isolate and lock off the machine before changing tools or clearing a jam
Only one person works the controls; keep hands outside the guarded area and stand clear of sheet whip
Sheet edges are sharp: deburr them and wear suitable gloves for handling
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Rolling, tacking and inspecting a cylinder with a formed end ring, with a quality report
practical2.brief: Your group will make a short cylinder for a small tank, to the assessor's drawing: about 300 mm outside diameter and 250 mm long, rolled from 3 mm mild steel plate, with a ring of 30 mm × 5 mm flat bar formed to fit around one end. First, as a group, work out the blank length from the mean diameter and the length of flat bar for the ring (show the working), and write a short plan and risk assessment. Mark out and cut the blank square. Make a template to the outside radius. Pre-bend both ends, then roll the cylinder in small steps: every member does at least one stage of the rolling while another member checks with the template. Tack the seam with the edges level. Measure the outside diameter in four directions at each end, work out the out-of-roundness and record it against the tolerance the assessor sets. Form the flat bar ring on the section rolls or around a former, check it on the cylinder, then fit and tack it square to the cylinder. Write a one-page quality report: the measurements, any faults, their likely causes and what you would change next time. Every member writes part of the report. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: 3 mm mild steel plate for the blank (about 250 mm × 935 mm)
30 mm × 5 mm mild steel flat bar, about 1 m
Guillotine, bending rolls, and section rolls or a ring former
Thin sheet or hardboard for the template
Welding set for tacking, with screens and welding PPE
Clamps, steel rule, tape measure, large calipers or a circumference tape, and a square
Calculation sheet, measurement sheet and report sheet
photos: The blank marked out and cut square
Rolling in progress, with the template being checked
The diameters being measured, with the readings recorded
The ring formed and tacked in place
checklist: Helped work out the blank and ring lengths and can explain why the mean diameter is used
Checked the trip bar or emergency stop before rolling, and kept hands, sleeves and rags clear of the nip
Rolled own stage in small steps and checked with the template
Measured the diameters accurately and worked out the out-of-roundness correctly
Helped form and fit the ring square to the cylinder
Took part in tacking or checking, wearing the correct PPE for welding
Wrote their part of the quality report clearly
Left the machines isolated and the area clean
safety: Keep hands, gloves, sleeves and rags well clear of the nip of the rolls; test the trip bar or emergency stop before use
Support the plate with a second person as it curves; plates are heavy and sharp
Isolate the rolls before adjusting or cleaning them
Tack weld only behind screens, with a helmet, gloves and flame-resistant clothing
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
